fact_check_log.claim: The Real Academia Española dictionary defines arras, in some marriage rites, as coins the couple give each other as a symbol of their union.
The RAE dictionary defines padrino as a man who accompanies someone receiving a Christian sacrament, with the example 'Seré el padrino de la boda'.
In the plural, padrinos means the padrino and the madrina together.

Mexico's national Indigenous peoples institute (INPI) describes how, in Nahua communities of the Sierra Norte de Puebla, a young man's grandparents accompany him to ask for the bride's hand; in their absence parents, baptism godparents, uncles or another trusted person may go.

INPI says that in these Nahua communities the bride's parents always answer that the proposal must be thought over, leading to at least three more visits, and that the decision is collective, involving the bride's parents, padrinos, uncles and grandparents.
INPI says that among Totonac communities today the man decides whom to marry and consults the woman first, then goes with his parents and baptism godparents to the petición de mano.
INPI states that, in the Nahua weddings it describes, the civil wedding must take place before the religious wedding.
INPI says that after the wedding both parents and padrinos remain responsible for watching over the new couple, and that before the party ends padrinos and parents give the couple advice.

A Nahuatl-Spanish story collection published on gob.mx describes a couple entering the church behind the priest, supported by padrinos of rings, arras and lazo, after being married by civil law the day before at the bride's home by the town authorities.

Smartraveller says some countries ask you to prove you are not already married, the most common documents being a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) or registry certificates, and advises contacting the destination's embassy or consulate for specifics.
A Mexican foreign ministry consulate page states that in Mexico a religious marriage does not replace the civil marriage, so a religious ceremony, if held, can be organised after the civil ceremony.
The same consulate page says marriage in Mexico is regulated locally by the states and that it is the couple's responsibility to check with the Registro Civil office nearest the ceremony location.
The consulate page says that after the civil ceremony the Registro Civil gives the couple an Acta de Matrimonio, which can be legalised and certified for use abroad.

An ethnographic study of weddings in Almoloya del Río (Estado de México) says the three moments of the pedimento de mano, the aviso, the acuerdo and the contento, have changed in their symbols but stayed unchanged in essence for at least the last two centuries.
In the same study, after a public dialogue between the parents the wedding date is set, generally with an engagement period of more than six months.
In the church wedding the study observed, the madrina de cojines hurried to place the cushions on the couple's kneelers before the other padrinos and guests entered, as the Ave María was sung.

The study records the couple's parents giving them their blessing at the altar, the padrinos de velación at the kneelers, and the other padrinos (of rings, arras, lazo, medals, bible and bouquet) taking places near the altar.
The padrinos of rings, arras, medals and lazo came forward for the priest to bless these symbols.
In the observed ceremony the groom received thirteen gold-coloured coins from the priest and placed them in the bride's hands, each speaking words about caring for the home.
In the observed ceremony the padrinos de lazo covered the groom's back with the veil and placed the lazo over it, while the mariachi sang religious songs; at the end the lazo was removed.
The study says parents and/or the couple choose the padrinos de lazo carefully: they must be a stable couple married in the church, as an example to their godchildren.
After the ceremony the couple went to the altar of the Virgin Mary, where the bride left at her feet the bouquet she carried in the Mass as an offering.

Britannica says family remains the most important element of Mexican society, that Mexicans generally keep strong links with extended family, including in-laws and 'adoptive' relatives, and that weddings are among the more lavish family-oriented events in Mexico.
Britannica says daily life in Mexico varies dramatically by socioeconomic level, ethnicity, region, rural versus urban setting and other factors.
Desde la Fe, the Archdiocese of Mexico's publication, lists the arras among the signs that are part of tradition, calling them a sign proper to Christian marriages in Spanish-speaking America.
Desde la Fe says the typical lazo consists of two rosaries joined to form one.
Desde la Fe says the nuptial blessing (bendición nupcial) comes after the Our Father, when the lazo is placed, and God's blessing is solemnly invoked.
Desde la Fe says candles are given by the padrinos de velación, those who watch over and care for the couple, ideally the baptism godparents.

Desde la Fe says the principal sign of the sacrament of Matrimony in the Catholic Church is the spouses' explicit consent, expressed through the words and vows of marriage, and distinguishes the important signs (holding hands, rings) from those that are more custom.
UNESCO lists 'Mariachi, string music, song and trumpet' (Mexico), inscribed in 2011 (6.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Page live, HTTP 200.

UNESCO describes mariachi as a traditional Mexican music and a fundamental element of Mexican culture; its repertoire includes serenades; the skill is passed down through performance at festive, religious and civil events. The element is tagged 'Wedding' in UNESCO's keyword list, but the description text itself does not mention weddings.

UNESCO describes traditional Mariachi groups (two or more members) wearing regional costumes adapted from the charro costume; modern Mariachi ensembles include trumpets, violins, the vihuela and guitarrón and may have four or more musicians.
The RAE dictionary defines 'tornaboda' as the day after the wedding, and as the party held on that day.

Smartraveller Mexico (updated 15 October 2026; still current at 6 November 2026): overall 'Exercise a high degree of caution'; 'Reconsider your need to travel' to Chiapas, Chihuahua, Colima, Guanajuato, Guerrero, Michoacán, north-western Durango, Sinaloa, Sonora, Tamaulipas and Zacatecas, each with listed exceptions.
Smartraveller Mexico: the hurricane and rainy season is June to November; tropical storms and hurricanes can happen in other months.
Smartraveller Mexico: same-sex relationships are legal and same-sex marriages are recognised; the country is conservative.

Smartraveller Mexico entry: Australians with a chipped ordinary passport visiting for tourism can use e-gates at a number of major airports and receive a printed QR code showing the days authorised; those without a chipped passport visiting for 180 days or less as tourists get a visa on arrival. Entry and exit conditions can change at short notice.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18 August 2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia; talk to a lawyer to confirm.

Smartraveller CNI page (last updated 1 October 2026): a CNI is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas; DFAT can't advise on another country's legal processes; some authorities only accept a CNI issued in their country, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it; ask whether an apostille is needed. DFAT charges fees.

Australian Embassy Mexico (live, HTTP 200): CNI applications are downloaded from Smartraveller and presented in person at the Embassy in Mexico City; honorary consulates do not provide notarial services, only the Embassy in Mexico does; payment by card only. The Embassy page lists a Cancún honorary consulate. (Fee amounts are published on the page but deliberately not recorded here.)

Zacatecas State Government (bulletin, 23 July 2023): the state tourism ministry (Secturz) supported 11 destination weddings with a callejoneada as an icebreaker before the ceremony, with guests touring the historic centre.

Mexico's Secretaría de Cultura catalogue (CID Alberto Beltrán, Fonoteca) holds a 1979 field recording of 'A la víbora de la mar' by the Banda de Música de Atlixco (Puebla), with notes that playing la víbora de la mar at weddings has become popular in Mexico, and that with the couple the 'víbora' stands for the problems they will face, and they must stay together without letting go.

Playa del Carmen municipal Registro Civil (Quintana Roo) publishes a 'Matrimonio Extranjero en oficina' procedure (updated 29/01/2026): book the date in advance; passports with certified Spanish translation if needed; proof of legal stay; apostilled and translated birth certificate where parents' names are to appear; ID for four witnesses (two per party); prenuptial medical certificate with lab results (valid 15 calendar days); application and declaration letters; municipal fee payment; certificate of not being a registered defaulting maintenance debtor. In person; resolution 20 business days. (Fee amount on the page deliberately not recorded.)

Britannica (last updated 10 October 2026): mariachi is a small Mexican ensemble of mostly stringed instruments; it emerged in the late 1700s or early 1800s in west-central Mexico; the word's etymology and early history are unknown.

Britannica: typical contemporary mariachi instruments are vihuela, guitarrón, six-string guitar, violins and trumpets (trumpets added in the early 20th century); since the early 20th century male bands typically wear traje de charro, the attire of the cowboys of Jalisco; women have played an increasing role since the 1940s, with all-female groups by the early 21st century.
